messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: How does lavaan compute the covariance of binary data?
parts:
You are not declaring your data to be binary / ordered categorical, and you are using an estimator (MLM) that assumes the data are continuous.  So lavaan is treating them as continuous data, using the Pearson formula to calculate covariance.  If you want lavaan to handle the data as categorical, you'll need to use DWLS estimation and declare which variables are ordered categorical.  See an example on the lavaan page:

http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/cat.html

Terry

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: How does lavaan compute the covariance of binary data?
parts: I cannot interpret the warning messages. I have no NAs or empty cells in my data.
They are telling you your model did not converge, and that the bivariate tables have zeros (not the same thing as missing values in the raw data).
Since items 1 - 4 have high skew values, I dropped them and ran the model again:

So items 1-4 have categories with very few observations, which means when you look at a contingency table (e.g., of item5 x item2, as one of the warnings points out), you will see cells with zeros (e.g., no one was observed to respond with category "a" to item5 AND with category "b" to item2).  This is a common problem with categorical data, made worse when N decreases or the number of items or categories increase.

Since item2 appears in all the warning messages about tables with empty cells, perhaps that is the item that causes the most trouble.  Try running the model with item2, but leave 1, 3, and 4 in, and see if the model converges.  "Skew" is not a problem for DWLS//WLS/WLSMV/ADF -- this family of estimators does not assume data are normal, or even symmetric.

Terry

messages.author: 89c9fc822e34b78c
messages.subject: Re: How does lavaan compute the covariance of binary data?
parts:
> What is the difference between DWLS and WLS? And what estimator is used
> to get the values in the "Robust" column when the estimator is DWLS? WLSM?

For categorical data, there are three possible 'least-squares' type
estimators: WLS, DWLS and ULS. The first is 'fully' weighted LS, the
second diagonally weighted LS, and ULS is unweighted LS.

Full WLS is not often used, since it requires a huge sample size.

Both DWLS and ULS can be run in 'robust' mode. This is the same as DWLS
(or ULS) but in addition, it gives you robust standard errors, and
either a mean adjusted (WLSM, ULSM) or mean and variance adjusted
(WLSMV, ULSMV) test statistic. They appear in the 'Robust' column.

The default is WLSMV.

Yves.

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: RE: How does lavaan compute the covariance of binary data?
parts:
Philipp—

     Start with regression under ordinary least squares estimation.  This estimation methods assumes homoscedasticity—equal residual variances. In attempting to minimize the overall sum of squared residuals, OLS weights the residuals equally.  If the homogeneity assumption is false, the OLS estimates may be inefficient.  Generalized least squares relaxes the homogeneity assumption and allows residual variances to differ.

     Now think about analysis of covariance structures under maximum likelihood estimation.  In analysis of covariance structures, the elements of the covariance matrix become the data points which the model must fit, and again there is the problem of minimizing an overall sum of squared residuals.  ML assumes (conditional) multivariate normality.  If observations are multivariate normal, then the variances and covariances among the elements of the covariance matrix follow a pattern.  Their values can be computed from the values within the covariance matrix itself.  We don’t even need the original data—just the covariance matrix.

     If the data are not multivariate normal, then this huge simplification does not follow, and we must use other means to weight the individual “data points” (the elements of the covariance matrix.  Under weighted least squares (WLS), we use the raw data to estimate these variances and covariances, but we must use higher order moments to do this, and that takes lots of data.

     Under diagonally weighted least squares (DWLS), we make the simplifying assumption that each element of the covariance matrix may have a different variance, but the covariances across elements are 0.  Under unweighted least squares (ULS), we return to OLS, in a sense, because we weights all elements of the covariance matrix equally, in effect assuming equal residual variances.  People choose the option not so much because they believe in equal residual variances, but because they lack the means to accurately estimate any better weights for the individual residual variances.  Moreover, we know that under certain conditions, in regression, equal weights or unit weights perform about as well as optimized regression weights (better against some criteria), while the use of unit weights avoids sampling variance in the estimates.

--Ed Rigdon

parts: Do you know how to inspect the covariance matrix when using WLSMV? The command inspect(fit, "sampstat")$cov seems to work when I'm using ML, however when using WLSMV it seems like I'm inspecting the correlation matrix.

I'm pretty sure WLS assumes that underlying each observed ordered indicator Y, there is a corresponding normally distributed latent variable Z, which software typically (arbitrarily, but for convenience) scales as standard normal.  The latent normal variable is hypothetically translated into observed ordered categories via thresholds (e.g., if Z < -0.5, Y = 0, otherwise 1).  So your covariance matrix when using ordered data IS an estimated polychoric correlation matrix simply because we assume the latent continuous variable is standard normal (i.e., with variance = 1).

From what I understand, WLS estimation for CFA with categorical indicators involves 3 steps:
  1. Estimate thresholds from sample proportions in each category
  2. Estimate polychoric correlations among indicators
  3. Fit structural model to estimated polychoric correlation matrix
I forget the citation for the source article, but I think you can find the one Yves uses by searching past posts on this forum involving WLS estimation.  Here is one article that provides some details.

https://www.statmodel.com/download/floracurran.pdf

Terry

The canonical reference is:

Muthén, B. (1984). A general structural equation model with dichotomous,
ordered categorical, and continuous latent variable indicators.
Psychometrika, 49, 115-132.

available from Muthén's website:
http://www.statmodel.com/bmuthen/psychometrics.htm

Yves.
